key_results: DSP is framed as the mathematics, algorithms, and techniques applied after real-world sensory signals are digitized. Its transferable core sits amid overlapping communication theory, numerical analysis, probability/statistics, analog processing, electronics, and decision theory rather than forming a sharply isolated field. [Chapter 1, The Roots of DSP and Fig. 1-2]

The same primitives recur across applications: multiplexing and compression in telecommunications, filtering and artificial reverberation in audio, matched pulse detection in radar/sonar, reflection analysis in seismology, and enhancement/reconstruction/compression in imaging. [Chapter 1, Telecommunications through Image Processing]

For a finite signal, the mean is the sample average; the unbiased sample variance divides the squared-deviation sum by N−1, and standard deviation is its square root. Standard deviation describes the AC fluctuation, whereas RMS includes both AC and DC and equals standard deviation only for zero-mean signals. [Chapter 2, Mean and Standard Deviation, Eqs. 2-1–2-2]

Running statistics need retain only N, the running sum, and the running sum of squares; mean and variance can be recomputed without storing or rescanning all samples. This form improves computational efficiency, though modern implementations should still consider numerical stability. [Chapter 2, Mean and Standard Deviation, Eq. 2-3 and Table 2-2]

Statistics describe an acquired finite record; probability describes the process that generated it. The typical error of a sample-mean estimate is σ/√N, and the Strong Law of Large Numbers guarantees convergence of the estimated mean as N grows. [Chapter 2, Signal versus Underlying Process, Eq. 2-4]

A histogram counts observed discrete values and sums to N; a probability mass function assigns discrete probabilities and sums to one; a probability density function applies to a continuous variable and has unit area. Binning makes histogram methods workable for large-valued or floating-point data. [Chapter 2, The Histogram, PMF and PDF, Eqs. 2-5–2-7, Figs. 2-4–2-7]

For a normal distribution, about 68%, 95%, and 99.75% of samples lie within ±1σ, ±2σ, and ±3σ. Its rapidly decaying tails explain why Gaussian random signals appear to have a practical peak-to-peak span of roughly 6–8σ even though they are theoretically unbounded. [Chapter 2, The Normal Distribution, Figs. 2-8–2-9]

The Central Limit Theorem explains why summing independent random contributions tends toward a Gaussian even when the component distributions are not Gaussian. A simple generator sums twelve uniform random variables, subtracts six, and then scales/shifts to the desired σ and mean. [Chapter 2, Digital Noise Generation, Fig. 2-10]

Precision is governed by random variation and can improve through averaging; accuracy is governed by systematic/calibration error and cannot. The diagnostic questions are whether averaging helps (precision) and whether calibration helps (accuracy). [Chapter 2, Precision and Accuracy]

Quantization is usually modeled as additive uniform noise between ±1/2 LSB, with zero mean and standard deviation 1/√12≈0.29 LSB. Independent analog and quantization noise combine by adding variances, so converter bit depth should be chosen relative to the noise already present and the noise the application can tolerate. [Chapter 3, Quantization, Fig. 3-1]

The additive-noise model fails for slowly varying or nearly constant inputs whose quantization error becomes signal-correlated. Dither deliberately adds noise so repeated samples toggle among adjacent codes; their average can then estimate sub-LSB signal levels—an explicit case where adding noise reveals information. [Chapter 3, Quantization, Figs. 3-2–3-3]

The sampling theorem requires an analog signal contain no components above half the sampling rate for unique reconstruction. Sampling replicates the analog spectrum at integer multiples of f_s; aliasing occurs when those replicas overlap, irreversibly merging frequencies. [Chapter 3, The Sampling Theorem, Figs. 3-4–3-5]

A practical DAC performs a zero-order hold rather than emitting ideal impulses. The hold multiplies the spectrum by sinc(f/f_s), causing about 36% high-frequency compensation at f_s/2 in an ideal reconstruction filter in addition to removal of spectral images above Nyquist. [Chapter 3, Digital-to-Analog Conversion, Eq. 3-1 and Fig. 3-6]

Analog and digital signals are constrained by the same information limits: amplitude resolution is limited by noise/quantization, and time resolution by bandwidth/sampling. A bandlimited analog signal and its properly sampled digital representation contain the same information; continuity does not imply infinite resolution. [Chapter 3, Digital-to-Analog Conversion]

Chebyshev, Butterworth, and Bessel analog filters optimize different objectives: transition sharpness, passband flatness, and step response respectively. Filter choice should follow how information is encoded—frequency-domain signals favor sharp rejection, while time-domain waveform shape favors Bessel-like transient fidelity. [Chapter 3, Analog Filters for Data Conversion and Selecting the Antialias Filter, Table 3-2]

For time-domain-encoded data, an aggressive antialias filter can destroy the feature being measured even while satisfying the sampling theorem. A Bessel filter trades gentle edge rounding for high-frequency rejection; no filter preserves sample values but leaves aliased interference and loses sub-sample timing cues. [Chapter 3, Selecting the Antialias Filter, Fig. 3-15]

Multirate conversion moves demanding filtering into software: sample fast behind a simple analog filter, digitally low-pass, then decimate; reverse with zero insertion, digital low-pass interpolation, DAC, and a simple reconstruction network. The chapter's voice example converts between 64 kHz and 8 kHz by factors of eight. [Chapter 3, Multirate Data Conversion]

Delta modulation encodes the slope of an input in the relative density of ones and zeros and is limited by the coupled choices of step size, slew rate, and data rate. Delta-sigma instead makes bit density track signal level; digital low-pass filtering and decimation turn its oversampled one-bit stream into conventional multibit samples. [Chapter 3, Single-Bit Data Conversion, Figs. 3-16–3-19]

A 16-bit two's-complement integer spans −32,768 to 32,767. IEEE single precision uses a sign bit, 8-bit biased exponent, and 23 stored fraction bits (with an implicit leading one); its relative spacing is about one part in 8–17 million, unlike the constant unit spacing of fixed point. [Chapter 4, Fixed Point through Number Precision, Figs. 4-1–4-3]

Roundoff can accumulate randomly as √K or coherently as K after K operations; because the sign pattern is algorithm-dependent and difficult to predict, the text recommends budgeting for additive worst-case accumulation. Integer counters avoid this class of drift entirely. [Chapter 4, Number Precision, Fig. 4-4 and Table 4-2]

Single-precision floating point exactly represents every integer through ±2²⁴≈±16.8 million. Powers-of-two fractions also have exact binary representations, whereas decimal increments such as 0.01 generally do not; loop control should therefore use integer indices. [Chapter 4, Number Precision]

Execution speed depends as much on data movement and architecture as arithmetic: cache reduces main-memory stalls, Harvard architectures fetch program and data simultaneously, pipelines overlap successive operations, and DSP processors provide dedicated multiply-accumulate hardware. [Chapter 4, Execution Speed: Hardware, Fig. 4-5]

A practical optimization hierarchy is to choose integer arithmetic when its range suffices, avoid repeated transcendental functions, precompute finite-domain functions in lookup tables, and benchmark the actual platform—especially I/O and graphics paths. [Chapter 4, Execution Speed: Programming Tips]

A DSP system is linear when it satisfies homogeneity and additivity; shift invariance is a separate property but is conventionally assumed in most DSP uses of 'linear system.' Shift invariance means a shifted input produces only the identical shift in the output. [Chapter 5, Requirements for Linearity, Figs. 5-2–5-4]

Sinusoidal fidelity is the defining intuition behind frequency response: a sinusoid passed through an LTI system remains a sinusoid at exactly the same frequency, changing only amplitude and phase. No other waveform has this universal eigenfunction property. [Chapter 5, Static Linearity and Sinusoidal Fidelity]

Superposition is the foundational strategy of DSP: decompose a complicated input into additive components, process each through the linear system, and synthesize the output components. The result equals processing the original signal directly. [Chapter 5, Superposition: the Foundation of DSP, Fig. 5-11]

Impulse decomposition leads to convolution; Fourier decomposition leads to spectral analysis; step, even/odd, and interlaced decompositions expose other useful structures. Interlaced decomposition is the recursive split underlying FFT speedups. [Chapter 5, Common Decompositions, Figs. 5-12–5-16]

Nonlinear systems are commonly handled by ignoring small nonlinearities, restricting operation to a small-signal approximately linear region, or applying a linearizing transform. Logarithms, for example, turn multiplication into addition in homomorphic processing. [Chapter 5, Alternatives to Linearity]

The impulse response completely characterizes an LTI system because an arbitrary input is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses. Convolution performs the corresponding sum of shifted, scaled impulse responses to produce the output. [Chapter 6, The Delta Function and Impulse Response through The Input-Side Algorithm]

For an N-sample input and M-sample impulse response, linear convolution has N+M−1 samples and obeys y[i]=Σ_{j=0}^{M−1}h[j]x[i−j], with undefined input samples treated as zero. The first and last M−1 outputs are boundary transients based on incomplete support. [Chapter 6, The Output-Side Algorithm, Eq. 6-1 and Fig. 6-10]

Input-side convolution distributes each input sample into a shifted/scaled impulse response; output-side convolution flips the impulse response and computes each output as a dot product. They are exactly the same operation and provide complementary implementation intuitions. [Chapter 6, The Input-Side Algorithm through The Sum of Weighted Inputs]

Convolving with a delta leaves a signal unchanged; scaled or shifted deltas implement gain and delay, and a sum of deltas implements echoes. First difference h=[1,−1] and running sum are discrete analogues of differentiation and integration and are inverse operations. [Chapter 7, Common Impulse Responses, Eqs. 7-1–7-5]

Convolution is commutative, associative, and distributive. Thus cascaded LTI systems may be reordered and replaced by convolution of their impulse responses, while parallel systems with summed outputs may be replaced by the sum of their impulse responses. [Chapter 7, Mathematical Properties, Eqs. 7-6–7-8]

Repeated self-convolution of a pulse converges rapidly toward a Gaussian; its width σ grows by the square root of the convolution count. This is the convolutional form of the Central Limit Theorem. [Chapter 7, Mathematical Properties, Fig. 7-12]

Cross-correlation measures similarity versus relative shift and peaks where a known target aligns with a received record. It equals convolution after reversing one operand and is the optimal linear detector of a known waveform in additive white noise—the matched-filter result. [Chapter 7, Correlation, Figs. 7-13–7-14]

Direct convolution costs N×M multiply-accumulates. The text uses this concrete cost to motivate short kernels, DSP hardware, and FFT convolution, which gives the identical result and can be hundreds of times faster for long records. [Chapter 7, Speed]

The real DFT represents an N-sample real record by N/2+1 cosine coefficients and N/2+1 sine coefficients, with special DC and Nyquist endpoint scaling; equivalently, polar form uses N/2+1 magnitudes and phases. Its basis frequency k completes exactly k cycles in N samples. [Chapter 8, Notation and Format of the Real DFT through Synthesis, Eqs. 8-1–8-4]

A finite input to the DFT is mathematically treated as one period of an infinitely repeated discrete signal. This convention is often physically meaningless but becomes essential for understanding circular symmetry and circular convolution. [Chapter 8, The Family of Fourier Transform]

DFT analysis is correlation with each cosine and sine basis function; synthesis rescales those components and adds them. The imaginary/sine convention includes a sign choice so that forward and inverse transforms align with the broader complex-transform convention. [Chapter 8, Synthesis through Duality]

Rectangular and polar frequency-domain forms contain identical information: magnitude is √(Re²+Im²), phase is atan2(Im,Re), and reconstruction uses Re=Mag cos θ and Im=Mag sin θ. Practical phase work must handle radians, quadrants, near-zero magnitude, 2π wrapping, and π jumps caused by a nonnegative magnitude definition. [Chapter 8, Polar Notation and Polar Nuisances, Eqs. 8-5–8-7]

Segment-averaged spectral analysis windows many fixed-length blocks, computes magnitude spectra, and averages them; random spectral noise falls as the square root of the number of averages while frequency resolution remains set by segment length. A longer single DFT improves bin spacing but not the noise level. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Fig. 9-1]

A window trades spectral leakage against resolution. Rectangular has the narrowest main lobe and largest sidelobes, Blackman has a wider lobe and lower sidelobes, Hamming lies between them, and flat-top sacrifices substantial resolution to measure peak amplitude accurately between DFT bins. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Figs. 9-4–9-5]

Frequency resolution has two distinct limits: DFT bin spacing and observation duration. Zero padding samples the same continuous spectral curve more densely but cannot provide the information that a longer nonzero record supplies for separating close tones. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Fig. 9-3]

A system's frequency response is the Fourier transform of its impulse response. Therefore x*h=y in time corresponds to XH=Y in frequency; zero-padding a finite impulse response provides denser samples of its continuous DTFT without changing the system. [Chapter 9, Frequency Response of Systems, Figs. 9-6–9-7]

DFT-domain multiplication implements circular convolution because the DFT treats time as periodic. To recover an N+M−1-sample linear convolution, both inputs must be zero-padded to at least that length before transformation. [Chapter 9, Convolution via the Frequency Domain, Figs. 9-8–9-9]
pedagogy: This shard is deliberately intuition-first and aimed at scientists and engineers who want DSP as a practical tool without making advanced mathematics a prerequisite. Smith introduces nearly every abstraction twice: first through a physical story or diagram, then through a compact equation and BASIC-like executable pseudocode. The sequence is unusually careful: applications motivate the field; probability and conversion establish what real data look like; computer-number behavior establishes implementation limits; linearity licenses decomposition; impulse decomposition becomes convolution; sinusoidal decomposition becomes the real DFT; and Chapter 9 reconnects both domains. Dense plots, 'machines' drawn as sliding dot products, and memorable analogies carry more explanatory load than formal proofs. The shard assumes algebra, elementary trigonometry, and basic science/engineering literacy; it teaches summation notation, probability vocabulary, binary numbers, and transform notation as needed and intentionally postpones complex numbers. There are no conventional end-of-chapter problem sets in Chapters 1–9. Instead, worked numerical examples, complete short programs, hardware/design scenarios, and interpretive figure sequences serve as exercises-by-inspection. Some hardware timings, component examples, and programming-language recommendations are historically dated, but the underlying lessons about quantization, memory traffic, numerical error, benchmarking, and algorithmic complexity remain useful.

gems: The T-carrier example turns multiplexing into arithmetic: each telephone voice is 8,000 samples/s × 8 bits = 64 kb/s; 24 voices fit into 1.544 Mb/s and travel about 6,000 feet on ordinary 22-gauge copper. [Chapter 1, Telecommunications]
Artificial reverberation is explained perceptually: echoes delayed by a few hundred milliseconds suggest a cathedral, while 10–20 ms delays suggest a modest room. [Chapter 1, Audio Processing]

Radar pulse length creates a clean engineering conflict—more energy extends detection range, but a longer pulse reduces range precision—then DSP pulse compression promises both. [Chapter 1, Echo Location]

The first CT scanner (1971) and the 1979 Hounsfield/Cormack Nobel Prize anchor tomography as a landmark DSP success that reconstructs cross-sectional images from many x-ray projections. [Chapter 1, Image Processing]

Random noise's practical peak-to-peak amplitude is about 6–8σ; the text dramatizes the Gaussian tail by noting that a >10σ event would be expected only for a few microseconds over roughly the age of the universe. [Chapter 2, The Normal Distribution]
The 'twelve uniforms' Gaussian generator is executable probability intuition: add twelve RND values, subtract six, then scale and shift. [Chapter 2, Digital Noise Generation, Fig. 2-10]

Dither's constant-voltage thought experiment is especially teachable: a true code of 3000.1 gives only 3000 without noise, but with dither about 90% of readings are 3000 and 10% are 3001, so 10,000 samples average near 3000.1. [Chapter 3, Quantization]

A 0.95-cycles/sample analog sine masquerades after sampling as a 0.05-cycles/sample sine—Smith's 'perfect crime' analogy for aliasing because the samples contain no clue to the original identity. [Chapter 3, The Sampling Theorem]

The 12-bit, 10 ksample/s antialias example shows why the top of a nominal Nyquist band is often unusable: an 8-pole Chebyshev must start its cutoff near 3.7 kHz to suppress content above 5 kHz. [Chapter 3, Analog Filters for Data Conversion]

The Mona Lisa line—viewers do not perceive an image as an 'interesting collection of sinusoids'—memorably separates time/space-domain encoding from audio's frequency-domain encoding and motivates different antialias priorities. [Chapter 3, Selecting the Antialias Filter]
A commercial delta-sigma ADC example operates its one-bit modulator at 6.4 MHz, uses a 246-tap FIR, and decimates 64:1 to deliver 16-bit samples at 100 kHz. [Chapter 3, Single-Bit Data Conversion]

The floating-loop bug prints 9.990133 and then skips the intended 10.00 endpoint; changing the control variable to an integer makes all 1,001 iterations exact. [Chapter 4, Number Precision, Table 4-2]

A lookup-table example maps each of 256 possible 8-bit voltage codes directly to resistor power; precomputation can be hundreds of times faster than evaluating P=V²/R repeatedly. [Chapter 4, Execution Speed: Programming Tips]

Aunt Edna's radish story and Uncle Bernie yelling at the dog emerge separately—not as 'Ednabernie'—to make additivity mean that superposed signals do not interact in a linear telephone system. [Chapter 5, Requirements for Linearity]

Multiplying 2041×4 by decomposing 2041 into 2000+40+1 is used as the everyday analogue of superposition: solve simple component problems and add the results. [Chapter 5, Superposition: the Foundation of DSP]

The convolution machine turns the index-heavy sum into a physical act: flip the impulse response, slide it, multiply aligned samples, and add, while the input-side story builds the same output from shifted impulse responses. [Chapter 6, The Input-Side Algorithm and The Output-Side Algorithm, Figs. 6-5–6-9]

A DC-removing high-pass convolution makes the first and last 30 output samples unusable, exposing edge effects as a practical consequence of incomplete data rather than a footnote about indexing. [Chapter 6, The Output-Side Algorithm, Fig. 6-10]

An intentionally irregular pulse looks strikingly Gaussian after only three self-convolutions, making the Central Limit Theorem visible as a signal operation. [Chapter 7, Mathematical Properties, Fig. 7-12]

Directly convolving one million samples with a 3,000-point impulse response is estimated at nearly an hour on the book's reference machine (and three days a decade earlier), a vivid setup for FFT convolution despite the dates of the hardware. [Chapter 7, Speed]

Fourier's 1807 claim that sinusoids represent periodic signals was rejected under Lagrange's objection about corners; the later resolution—arbitrarily close with zero-energy difference—previews the Gibbs effect. [Chapter 8, The Family of Fourier Transform]

The phase 'nuisance' checklist reads like a debugging guide: define π, use quadrant-aware arctangent, distrust phase where magnitude vanishes, unwrap 2π jumps, and recognize artificial π flips. [Chapter 8, Polar Nuisances]

The simulated undersea microphone spectrum encodes a detective story: a 13 Hz fundamental and harmonics could be a three-bladed propeller turning at 4.33 revolutions/s amid white noise, 1/f noise, 60 Hz hum, and antialias roll-off. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Fig. 9-2]

The 256-sample signal plus 51-sample kernel should produce 306 samples; forcing the calculation through a 256-point DFT wraps 50 tail samples into the front, making circular convolution literally visible. [Chapter 9, Convolution via the Frequency Domain, Fig. 9-9]
